1:
What 'elder' means is the first question, and the witnesses settle it alike. Gill argues for age, not office: elders by office get rules of their own later, and the word stands opposed here not to a private member but to young men in age. Clarke agrees it is taken in its natural sense of one advanced in years, whereas at the seventeenth verse it carries its ecclesiastical meaning; Ellicott finds the point settled by the parallel clause on elder women; Robertson, that the dative bears the usual sense of an older man. On the verb they are agreed and unusually vivid. Gill observes that it signifies to smite or strike, so that the Arabic renders it 'do not strike an elder' — not with the hand but with the tongue, hard words being as heavy blows. Clarke glosses it as do not treat them harshly, nor with magisterial austerity. Robertson identifies an ingressive aorist subjunctive after a negative, a prohibition against committing the act at all, from a verb meaning to strike upon, found only here in the New Testament and figuratively of words, not fists.

Ellicott and Calvin both explain why a young minister in particular needed the rule. Ellicott notes the turn the letter takes: from the public duties of the superintending presbyter the Apostle passes to the private relations one in Timothy's position ought to keep with individual members — and the first thing he warns him against is a misplaced zeal. The ardent young servant of Christ would see with sorrow the shortcomings of many an elder member of his flock, and, forgetting to allow for previous training, thought and habits, would be likely, unwisely and unfairly, to find fault; let him use respectful and affectionate entreaties, after the manner of a son and not of an official. Calvin puts it as a matter of dosage. Correction is a medicine which always has some bitterness, and is consequently disagreeable; and Timothy being young, his severity would have been the less tolerable unmoderated. Yet he is careful to say the Apostle does not wish old men indulged so as to sin with impunity — only that some respect be paid to their age, that they may the more patiently bear admonition. The vinegar must always be mingled with the oil, though reverence is due to older persons and equals treated with brotherly gentleness. Wesley compresses it into a clause: rebuke not, considering your own youth, with such severity as would otherwise be proper.

Henry sets out the four classes as one rule of proportion. Ministers are reprovers by office, the least pleasing part of it, and a great difference is to be made according to the age and circumstances of those rebuked. Elders must not be rebuked sharply nor magisterially, respect being had to the dignity of their years and place, entreaty being the likeliest way to win upon them; the younger as brethren, with love and tenderness, not as one desirous to spy faults but willing to make the best of them; the elder women as mothers, the younger as sisters, with all purity. On that last phrase Barnes is searching. Nothing, he says, could be more characteristic of Paul, or show a deeper acquaintance with human nature: the Apostle knew the danger besetting a youthful minister whose duty it was to admonish a youthful female, and the scandal he might incur at the slightest departure from purity and propriety in performing his office. He was to guard his heart with more than common vigilance, and indulge in no word, look or action which could possibly be construed as manifesting an improper state of feeling. Robertson makes a maxim of it — no behaviour will so easily make or mar the young preacher as his conduct with young women; and Clarke adds that a minister should labour to keep members in, not expel them.
3:
What 'honour' means here is settled quickly and unanimously: it means money. Clarke notes that one sense of the verb is to support or sustain, and holds that it is most obviously to be taken so here — provide for those widows especially which are widows indeed, persons truly destitute, being aged and helpless, having neither children nor friends to take care of them, and behaving as becomes their destitute state. Gill agrees, but first rules out an alternative: the honour is not a putting of them into the office of a deaconess, since that could be the case of some only, whereas this honour is due to all that are really widows. It therefore means external honour and respect shown by words and actions, and especially an honourable provision and maintenance — and Gill adds that with the Jews the giving of gifts and making of presents to a person was itself called honour. Wesley reduces the whole to four words: maintain out of the public stock.

Henry, Barnes and Ellicott are more interested in the institution behind the command. Henry takes the passage as directions concerning the taking of widows into the number of those employed by the church and maintained from its funds, and reports that there was in those times an office in the church in which widows were employed, to tend the sick and the aged and to look to them under the direction of the deacons — an arrangement whose beginnings appear in the church's first days, when the Grecians thought their widows neglected in the daily ministration. Barnes explains why the work fell to women of that age and condition. The intercourse of the sexes was much more circumscribed in oriental countries than among us, and access to the female members of the church much less free, so that there might have been a special propriety in entrusting the duty of watching over the younger to the more aged; and the duty would naturally be committed to those who had not the care of families, and who, while maintained by the church, might be rendering a valuable service to it. Ellicott sets it in a wider frame, arguing that Christianity had in thirty years developed a perfectly new existence for women: until Christ taught the universal duty of charity, women had no recognised public occupation, and their secluded and in many respects degraded life in the old world was in great measure owing to that fact.

The fourth verse turns from the church's duty to the family's, and the first thing to settle is who is meant. Barnes and Ellicott agree that the old rendering misleads: the word now commonly means the son of a brother or sister, but the Greek denotes those sprung or born of, embracing only those in a direct line, so that it should be rendered grandchildren and would not properly include nephews and nieces at all. Ellicott reads the verse as a warning against allowing the Church to be burdened with what others ought to bear, put in the form of a pressing reminder to the children and grandchildren of a destitute widow — a solemn and imperative duty, not to be evaded by any bearing the Christian name, and one to which an especial blessing is promised. Clarke supplies the ground of the obligation plainly: let them learn to give benefit for benefit, since your parents supported and nourished you when you were young and helpless, and you ought therefore to support them when they are old and destitute; and he hears in it an allusion to the fifth commandment. Robertson makes the sharpest application, refusing any religious escape from the duty — there is no corban business here, and no acts of piety toward God will make up for impiety towards parents. Filial piety is primary, he adds, unless parents interfere with duty to Christ.
5:
The widow indeed is defined by two things, her isolation and her praying. Barnes warns against reading too much into the first: the word rendered desolate means solitary or alone, and does not carry the idea of discomfort we attach to the English word — the sense is that she had no children or descendants on whom she could depend. Having no one else to look to, destitute of husband, children and property, she feels her dependence and steadily looks to God. Robertson confirms the grammar: the participle is a perfect passive, left alone, a verb found here only in the New Testament, describing one without husband, children or close kin; the verb of hoping is a perfect active, she has placed her hope on God and keeps it there. On the last phrase he enters a caution of his own — the words are genitive, by night and by day, and Paul does not say she should pray all night and all day. Clarke draws the two halves together: finding she has no other helper, she continues in prayer and supplication, that she may derive from God what in the course of his providence he has deprived her of among men.

Against her stands the widow who lives in pleasure, and the witnesses are careful about how bad that is. Barnes notes that the Greek word occurs only once elsewhere in the New Testament, and that it properly means to live in luxury, voluptuously, indulging freely in eating and drinking: it does not indicate grossly criminal pleasures, but the kind of pleasure connected with luxurious living and with pampering the appetites. It is probable, he adds, that in the apostle's time there were professedly Christian widows who lived so, as there are such professing Christians in every age. Clarke reaches the same judgment and illustrates it unexpectedly, since the word is used of petted and spoiled children; he quotes an ancient letter on the boy who weeps if he has not food when and as he pleases, who must have dainties and sweetmeats, who complains of fatigue if the weather be hot and trembles if it be cold, and is enraged if everything be not provided to his wish. Wesley is briefest and most exact: delicately, voluptuously, in elegant, regular sensuality — though not in the use of any such pleasures as are unlawful in themselves.

Ellicott takes up the paradox in which the contrast ends. It is a thoroughly Pauline thought, he says, set forth in other language in the Roman Epistle, that those who live after the flesh shall die; and the widow who could so forget her sorrow and her duty is a living corpse, sharply contrasted with her far happier sister who, dead to the pleasures of the flesh and living a life of prayer and self-denial, may in the true sense be spoken of as living. He notes that the greatest of the Greek poets used the same figure to the opposite end, counting the man who gives up pleasures a living corpse. On the charge that follows, Clarke makes a point the others miss: the words are spoken not of the widows only but of the Church or its officers, and cannot be restricted to the widows, since the adjective is both masculine and feminine. Ellicott hears in the same clause something about the congregation's past, suggesting a hint that the former life of many of these women converts had been very different from the life loved of Christ, and that in their new profession there was urgent need of watchfulness not to give any occasion to slanderous tongues. Gill lists what is being charged: the rebuking of persons of different age and sex, the maintenance of widows, the duty of children to provide for helpless parents, and the duty of widows to trust in God.
8:
Chrysostom takes the verse as a refutation of a whole way of thinking about salvation. Many consider their own virtue sufficient, and that if they duly regulate their own life nothing further is wanting; but in this they greatly err, as the man who buried his one talent proves, for he brought it back not diminished but entire, just as delivered to him. The provision the Apostle speaks of, he insists, is universal, relating to the soul as well as the body, since both are to be provided for. He then presses the absurdity of the alternative. If a man deserts those united to him by ties of kindred, how shall he be affectionate towards others? Will it not look like vainglory, when in benefiting others he slights his own relations? And what will be said if, instructing others, he neglects his own — will it not be said that these Christians are affectionate indeed, who neglect their own relatives? He also gives the reason the comparison with the infidel bites: the unbeliever, if he benefits not aliens, at least does not neglect his near kindred. Gill states the duty concretely — not only for wife and children, but for parents grown old and unable to help themselves.

How wide the obligation reaches is the next question, and the answers widen it. Barnes takes 'his own' to mean those naturally dependent on a man, whether they live in his immediate family or not, since many distant relatives may depend on our aid besides those under our roof; and he draws out the force of the verb, that a man is to think beforehand of the probable wants of his family and make arrangements to meet them — as God provides for our wants, seeing beforehand what we shall need. Ellicott sees the circle enlarged by the second clause: the prosperous man who professes to love Christ is bound not merely to do his best for his nearest relations, such as his mother and grandmother, but to assist those of his own house — a term taking in far more distant relatives, and even dependents of the family fallen into poverty. Clarke keeps the two steps plainly, glossing 'his own' as his people or relatives, and 'those of his own house' as his family, or a poor widow or relative living under his roof.

The closing comparison is the sharpest thing in the chapter. Clarke explains why an unbeliever makes the standard: the dictates of nature lead men to feel for and provide for their own families, and heathen writers are full of maxims of the kind — Tacitus, that nature dictates that to every one his own children and relatives should be most dear, and Cicero, that every man should take care of his own. Robertson puts it as a contradiction between profession and act: his act of impiety belies his claim to the faith, and the comparative sets him below one who makes no profession of piety at all. Ellicott adds that faith, considered as a rule of life, is practically denied by one who neglects these duties, since faith works by love; and he sees a real situation behind the warning, for men and women were persuading themselves that the promises of Christians could be won by a mere profession of faith, apart from any loving consideration for others — there being evidently in Ephesus not a few professed believers who, possessed of wealth, could calmly look on while their relations languished in the deepest poverty. Wesley turns the verse against a use commonly made of it: what has this to do with heaping up money for our children, for which it is so impertinently alleged? All men have their reasons for laying up money — one will go to hell for fear of want, another acts like a heathen lest he be worse than an infidel.
9:
What exactly the widow is enrolled into divides the witnesses. Robertson translates the verb as to set down in an official list, a word found only here in the New Testament, and takes the list of genuine widows to have had church work attached to it, such as care for the sick and the orphans. Ellicott reconstructs an institution: here and here only in the New Testament is it alluded to, but the instructions are so definite that it is impossible not to assume, in some if not all of the great churches, an official band of workers consisting of widows carefully selected from the congregation, of advanced age and specially distinguished for devotion, each of a high and stainless reputation — a distinct order, formally entered on the Church's list. Gill dissents. Some understand the words of those made deaconesses, and the Arabic renders it so, but the former sense is best, since the Apostle is still speaking of widows to be relieved. He gives practical reasons for the age limit: under sixty it might be supposed they would marry and so not be desolate, or would be capable of labour and so of maintaining themselves; and sixty was by the Jews reckoned old age. Henry states the principle the limit serves — many are proper objects of charity who yet ought not to be employed in public services.

On the phrase 'the wife of one man' three readings stand side by side. Clarke lists them all: having lived in conjugal fidelity with her husband; or having had but one husband at a time; or, according to others, having never been married more than once. The first, he says, is the opinion of some of the most eminent Greek fathers, and appears most consistent with the scope of the place and with truth. Robertson takes the third without hesitation — widows on this list must not have married a second time — though he grants the interpretation is less clear in the parallel requirements for bishops and deacons. Wesley takes the widest sense, glossing it as having lived in lawful marriage, whether with one or more persons successively; and he adds that afterwards such widows were admitted at forty, if they were eminent for holiness.

The list of qualifying works is read as a description of habit rather than a checklist. Barnes takes 'brought up children' of her own or others', the point being that she has done it well, and reads the lodging of strangers as hospitality, a virtue greatly commended in Scripture. On the washing of the saints' feet he is careful: it is uncertain whether this is literal or denotes offices of a humble and self-denying kind, and since washing a guest's feet was a rite of hospitality in the East, Paul may have meant it literally — but there is not the slightest evidence that he refers to it as a religious rite or ordinance, any more than to the bringing up of children. Clarke supplies the background: it was customary among the Gentiles to expose their children when too poor to provide for them, and pious people took these up and fed and clothed and educated them, so the phrase may refer to the children of others brought up in the Christian faith by Christian women. Washing the feet he likewise explains from custom, an office of humanity shown to strangers and travellers in eastern countries, who, walking barefoot or with only a sort of sole, needed it at journey's end. Ellicott guards the first item against a wooden reading: it must not be supposed that St. Paul meant to exclude childless women from the order — only that the candidate must be known as one who loves children, and would gladly discharge any duties to the little orphans of the flock entrusted to her.
11:
The verb translated 'wax wanton' provokes the chapter's sharpest philological disagreement. Barnes protests that the English conveys a thought by no means in the original, and one unjust both to the apostle and to the younger widows: in the Greek there is no idea of wantonness in the sense of lasciviousness or lewdness, nor was that sense essential to the English word when the translation was made, since 'wanton' then meant roving in gaiety or sport, flying loosely, playing in the wind. Clarke reaches the same sense by another route, deriving the compound from an intensive and a verb meaning to act luxuriously, and beyond that from words meaning to remove and the rein — a metaphor from a pampered horse whose rein has been taken from his mouth, so that nothing is left to check or confine him. Robertson goes the other way, glossing the verb as to feel the impulse of sexual desire; it is a late compound found only here and in Ignatius, and he records Souter's rendering, to exercise youthful vigour against Christ.

Why the younger were refused is answered from several directions. Chrysostom notices what the Apostle does not say, and thinks the silence deliberate: concerning virgins, though the case of their falling is a much more gross one, he has said nothing of this kind, and rightly, for they had enrolled themselves on higher views, and the work with them proceeded from a greater elevation of mind — the receiving of strangers and washing of the saints' feet being represented, in their case, as attending upon the Lord without distraction. Ellicott insists the exclusion is from office only: it by no means shuts the younger women out from the alms of the Church if they were in need, but wisely excluded them from a position and duties which they might covet in their first days of grief, but of which, as experience had shown the Apostle, they not unfrequently wearied — those who put their hands to the plough and afterwards looked back being a hindrance to the Church's work, and in some cases a subject of scandal. Gill gives the practical grounds, that they are fit for labour and can take care of themselves, and that they may marry and so have husbands to keep them; and Clarke supplies what makes the second a difficulty, that those received into such a list probably promised to abide in their widowhood — the Apostle condemning remarriage not as a crime in itself, but as contrary to their engagement.

What is threatened, and what is broken, are both softened here. Ellicott objects to the received rendering: the word means judgment, not necessarily damnation, and the Greek is often thus unhappily translated, the context deciding in each case whether the judgment is favourable or not. Here it means that those who later give up a work undertaken for their Master's sake expose themselves to a searching judgment, which will sift the reasons that induced them to forsake the begun toil, and which, if those reasons prove unsatisfactory, will be unfavourable. Robertson explains the other phrase in the same key, taking 'their first faith' as their first pledge or contract to Christ, so that breaking it is like breaking the marriage contract; evidently one pledge on joining the order was not to marry, and he notes the suggestion that enrolment amounted to a kind of ordination. Wesley turns the phrase inward. They have deserted their trust in God, he says, and acted contrary to their first conviction, that wholly to devote themselves to his service was the most excellent way — and when we first receive power to believe, does not the Spirit generally point out what are the most excellent things, and give us a holy resolution to walk in the highest degree of Christian severity? How unwise are we, he concludes, ever to sink below it.
13:
Clarke takes the catalogue of faults one word at a time. They learn to be idle: they do not love work, and they will not work. Wandering from house to house is gadding and gossiping, never contented with home, always visiting. If it went no farther this would be intolerable, but they are tattlers — tale-bearers, whisperers, all noise and no work; busybodies, who mind every one's business but their own; speakers of things they ought not, meaning lies, slanders and calumnies, backbiting their neighbours and sowing the seed of dissension. Barnes cautions against reading this as a judgment on widows as such: the apostle does not mean that widows are naturally disposed to be idle, but that in the situation referred to there would be danger of it, there being a security in the age and settled habits of the older which there could not be in their case. Ellicott finds the danger in the work itself: their very occupation would become a snare, since going about the dwellings to console and instruct would give them, once their minds were no longer turned exclusively to religious thoughts, many an opportunity of wasting precious hours in frivolous, if not harmful, conversation. Robertson notes that there is no verb 'to be' in the Greek phrase, and calls the picture of wandering around the houses a vivid one of idle tattlers.

The remedy prescribed is marriage, and Clarke will not let the point be blurred: since the preceding discourse concerned the younger widows, by the younger women he means them, and here the apostle, so far from forbidding second marriages, positively enjoins or at least recommends them. And what man of sense, Clarke asks, could have done otherwise? It is no sin to marry, bear children and take care of a family, but it is a sin in every case to be idle. Ellicott reads the counsel as a warning against premature asceticism: the Apostle wills that the younger widows should not, in the first fervour of their zeal and while borne down by sorrow, attempt anything like an ascetic life which they would probably tire of, and so in the long run injure rather than benefit the cause of Christ. St. Paul's practical mind, he adds, has left us no impossible rules of perfection. Robertson notices what the third verb concedes: the wife is here put as ruler of the household, a proper recognition of her influence, and what Liddon called a new and improved position. Wesley states the practical effect: then will they have sufficient employment of their own, and give no occasion of reproach to the adversary, whether Jew or heathen.

That some had already failed is the reason for all of it. The backsliding of these nameless ones had probably been the immediate occasion of the directions to Timothy; and though they had worked such great mischief to the cause of Christ, St. Paul, with his tender grace, forbore to name any — they had undertaken a task too severe for them, and had miserably failed. Gill widens the phrase into a rule: everyone who apostatizes from a profession of Christ and follows either false teachers, such as the Gnostics who condemned marriage, or any impure way of life, may be said to turn aside after Satan. Clarke reduces the same warning to a sentence worth remembering: slight deviations, in the first instance, from a right line may lead at last to an infinite distance from Christ. On the final verse Robertson identifies who is addressed: the believing woman who has widows is one of the household-rulers of the previous verse, and the widows are those dependent on her, candidates for the roll. Clarke states the purpose plainly — let such relieve their own and not burden the Church, that the funds may be spared for the widows employed in its service, teaching children and visiting the sick.
17:
Gill clears the ground by elimination, 'elder' having just been used in another sense. These are not elders in age, for those were noticed at the chapter's opening, and these are described as rulers and labourers in the word. They are not civil magistrates, such as were called the elders of Israel, for it belongs to none of these to preach the Gospel. They are not deacons, since deacons are never called elders in Scripture, their work is serving tables and not ruling, and the ministry of the word does not belong to them. Nor are they lay elders who rule but teach not, since Gill holds there are no such officers in the churches of Christ, whose only officers are elders and deacons. Robertson settles the question by usage, taking the word of position in the same sense as bishop, and pointing to passages where men called elders in one verse are called bishops in the next. Clarke cites Macknight, that in the first age the name was given to all who exercised any sacred office in the Church.

That the honour in question is money is agreed with unusual frankness. Clarke reports that almost every critic of note allows the word to signify reward, stipend or wages: let him have a larger salary who rules well — and the reason is that in discharging his office such a man must be at expense in proportion to his diligence, visiting and relieving the sick, lodging strangers, and keeping the hospitality required of every bishop. Robertson canvasses the proposals: White suggests remuneration rather than honour, Liddon honorarium as covering both honour and pay, Wetstein cites soldiers receiving double pay for unusual services, and some suggest twice the pay given the enrolled widows. Wesley reads it as a more abundant provision, seeing such men employ it all to the glory of God — then adds a piece of church history against his own argument. Since the most laborious and disinterested men were put into these offices, whatever any one had to bestow in life or death was lodged in their hands for the poor; by this means churchmen became very rich in after ages, but as the donors' design was something else, there is the highest reason why it should be disposed of according to their pious intent.

The verse has long been the battleground of the ruling elder, and Henry states the case against his own tradition candidly. The presbytery ruled, he says, and the same men who ruled laboured in the word and doctrine: they had not one to preach to them and another to rule them, but one and the same person did both. Some have imagined that by the elders that rule well the apostle means lay-elders, employed in ruling but not teaching, concerned in church government but not with the word and sacraments — and Henry confesses this the plainest text of scripture to be found for such an opinion. Yet he cannot take it: it seems strange that mere ruling elders should be worth double honour, when the apostle preferred preaching to baptizing and would much more prefer it to ruling; and stranger still that he should take no notice of such officers where he treats of church officers directly. Barnes approaches the problem historically: the word was in familiar use among the Jews for the body of men who presided in the synagogue, and probably not precisely the same organisation was followed in every place where a church was established. Ellicott presses what the passage implies about Timothy's own powers: to use the title of Bishop in the ecclesiastical sense would be as yet an anachronism, but one in his position evidently distributed the grades of honour and remuneration among the presbyteral order, and to him as presiding elder belonged the office of supreme judge in all matters ecclesiastical and moral.
18:
The two proofs the Apostle offers settle the meaning of the preceding verse, and Clarke says so outright: the quotation about the ox is a manifest proof that by honour he meant salary or wages. Clarke then turns the argument both ways. The maintenance of every man in the Church should be in proportion to his own labour and his family's necessities; he that does no work should have no wages; and in the Church of Christ there never can be a sinecure. They who minister at the altar should live by the altar, and the ox that treadeth out the corn should not be muzzled — but the altar should not support him who does not minister at it, and if the ox will not tread out the corn, let him go to the common or be muzzled. Ellicott draws the inference from lesser to greater: if the well-known law of Israel specially reminded them that the very animals which laboured for them were not to be kept from the fruits of their labour, surely men who devoted themselves as God's servants to their fellows should be treated with all liberality.

The second quotation raises a textual question the witnesses answer differently. Barnes observes that the saying is found substantially in Matthew and Luke, that it occurs nowhere in the Old Testament, and that the apostle nevertheless adduces it as a quotation from the Scriptures and as authority — from which it would seem probable he had seen one of those Gospels and regarded the book as Scripture. Robertson is less willing to conclude. The words occur in precisely this form in Luke, and elsewhere Paul plainly means that Jesus had so ordained; but whether he quotes here an unwritten saying of Jesus, or Luke's Gospel, or the collection of sayings, there is no way to decide. Ellicott allows the possibility that the Apostle combines a quotation from a Gospel with one from Deuteronomy under the single formula, but thinks it hardly likely.

The rule about accusations is read by all as a special protection, and the reason given is the same everywhere. Clarke states it plainly: be very cautious of receiving evil reports against those whose business it is to preach to others and correct their vices, since men whose office it is to correct others will usually have many enemies. He finds a Roman parallel — a plebeian might be condemned on the deposition of one credible witness, but it required two to convict a senator — and Wesley finds a Mosaic one, that by the law a private person might be cited, though not condemned, on the testimony of a single witness, whereas the Apostle forbids an elder to be even cited on such evidence, his reputation being of more importance than another's. Ellicott names the likely sources of such charges, which owe much to jealousy, party feeling and suspected doctrinal error. But the protection is not a shelter, and Gill is emphatic that the Apostle was far from screening wicked ministers guilty of flagitious crimes: the words chiefly regard elders who sin, who continue to sin, who live in some notorious sin which is evident and known, to the great scandal of religion — and he notes that some read the clause as 'them that sin before all, rebuke'. Such men are not merely to be admonished once and again but degraded from office and cast out publicly, which the Arabic version renders 'before the congregation'. Barnes marks the limit of that power: it extends only to spiritual censures, there being no power given of inflicting punishment by fine or imprisonment. Robertson adds the qualification that keeps it from becoming something else — public rebuke when there is a clear case, not promiscuous gossip.
21:
Chrysostom explains why the solemnity comes just here. Having spoken of bishops and deacons, of widows and elders, and shown how great the authority of a bishop was, the Apostle now comes to judgment, and adds this charge. Thus fearfully does he charge him; for though Timothy was his beloved son, he did not therefore stand in awe of him — since he was not ashamed to say of himself that he feared lest, having preached to others, he should be a castaway, much less would he be ashamed in Timothy's case. He calls the Father and the Son to witness; and the elect angels Chrysostom explains from great moderation, comparing Moses calling heaven and earth to witness. Why they are called elect divides the others. Clarke reports the received view, that the word distinguishes those who stood when the rest fell from their first estate, the former elect or approved and the latter reprobate — though perhaps nothing else is meant than the angels chosen out by the Lord himself to be ministering servants to the Church. Robertson takes the first sense flatly: they are the holy angels who kept their own principality and did not sin.

Barnes dwells on the verb, which means properly to call to witness, then to affirm with solemn attestations, then to admonish earnestly — a word implying that the subject is of great importance. Paul gives the charge as in the presence of God, of the Redeemer and of the elect angels, to secure the solemnity such holy witnesses must bring; and Barnes presses it home, since no one can prove that the angels and the departed spirits of holy men are not witnesses of what we do, and it is right to urge duty as if the eye of a departed father or mother were fixed upon us. On the two conditions, Clarke is practical: promote no man's cause, and make not up thy mind on any case till thou hast weighed both sides and heard both parties with their witnesses, then act impartially as the matter appears proved. Wesley says the same in fewer words — pass no sentence till the cause is fully heard, and none for or against any one — adding that the Apostle here looks through his own labours and through time itself, and seems to stand as one already in eternity.

What the laying on of hands refers to is the chapter's last dispute, and it goes unresolved. Gill argues for ordination alone: the phrase cannot mean the removing of censures from offenders on their repentance, which in later times has indeed been done by imposition of hands, since no such custom obtained in the apostle's time and Scripture never signifies the taking off of censures by this phrase. Barnes agrees that the obvious meaning is ordination, and draws the caution — Timothy should not be hasty in an act so important as introducing men to the ministry, but should take time to give them a fair trial of their piety, and not ordain a man merely because he showed piety, or burned with zeal, or thought himself qualified. Ellicott takes the wider view: while the command refers primarily to ordination it no doubt also includes the laying on of hands customary on the absolution of penitents, and to limit it to ordination alone would imply a greater corruption in the church at that early date than is credible. Robertson declines to choose: it is not clear whether the case is that of ministers just ordained, or a warning against hasty ordination of untried men, or the restoration of deposed ministers — the prohibition suits either, or both. Clarke draws the moral for those who ordain: it is a sin for an improper person to thrust himself into the sacred office, and he partakes of that sin who introduces him, helps him forward, or sanctions him.
23:
Why the verse stands here at all is the first difficulty, and the answers converge on an argument about the letter's authenticity. Barnes reports that much difficulty has been felt about the connection, so much that many have supposed the verse displaced; but he thinks it was introduced because Paul was suddenly impressed with the arduous nature of the ministerial office, as a man writing on the duties of the ministry is likely to be. The labours enjoined demanded all of a man's time, and the care incident to such a charge would be likely to prostrate the frame and injure the health — and then the Apostle remembered that Timothy was yet but a youth, of feeble constitution, frequently ill, and abstemious by his own rule. Clarke reports the same objection, that the verse seems to several learned critics strangely inserted here and might have been a marginal note added on recollecting Timothy's precarious health, and rejects it: he believes it in its proper place, and not less necessary than the directions around it. Ellicott turns the oddity into evidence. Those who argue that this Epistle was the artificial composition of a later age have no little difficulty in accounting for such a command; it can only be explained on the supposition that the letter was truly written by Paul to Timothy in all freedom and love — for no ecclesiastical forger of the second or third century would have dreamed, or dared, to weave such a charge into such an Epistle.

What is prescribed, and how far it goes, is handled with equal care. Robertson renders the first clause as be no longer a water-drinker, a verb found only here in the New Testament, and insists on the limit: this is not a call away from asceticism as such, but the urging of some wine in Timothy's peculiar physical condition — a medical prescription for this case, the emphasis falling on 'a little'. Timothy, he concludes, was a semi-invalid. Gill balances the two duties: it was commendable to keep under his body by abstemious living, yet proper that he take care of his health, lest it be impaired by too much severity and he be made incapable of the work of the Lord — and it seems his long and exclusive use of water had been prejudicial. Clarke explains where such a habit came from: the priests under the Mosaic law were forbidden wine while performing sacred rites, on pain of death; the same held among the Egyptian priests, and among the Romans wine was forbidden particularly to women and the young.

Cyril of Jerusalem takes the verse into a wider argument about food and fasting, using it to restrain both parties at once. Concerning food, he says, let these be your ordinances, since in the matter of meats also many stumble: some deal indifferently with things offered to idols, while others discipline themselves but condemn those who eat — men's souls being defiled in different ways from ignorance of the reasons for eating and not eating. He then states what fasting is for, which is not contempt of the creature: we fast by abstaining from wine and flesh, not because we abhor them as abominations, but because we look for our reward — that having scorned things sensible we may enjoy a spiritual feast, and having sown in tears may reap in joy in the world to come. From this he draws the double prohibition that makes the verse his: despise not those who eat, and who because of the weakness of their bodies partake of food, nor blame those who use a little wine for their stomach's sake and their often infirmities; neither condemn the men as sinners, nor abhor the flesh as strange food. Ellicott adds that the reminder was suggested by the Apostle's own words just before, telling Timothy to keep himself pure.
24:
The closing verses return to the caution about ordaining, and Clarke sorts the candidates in three. Some he knew nothing of but that they professed Christianity, and these were to be tried before appointment; some he knew fully in faith and piety, and their usefulness was well known; and some had lives not at all, or but partially, reformed, still unchanged in heart and unholy in life. The sins of these last were known to all, and it is they who go before to judgment; with them he could have no difficulty. The first class was the hard one, since hypocrites might be among them whose sins could not be known until after they were in the sacred office — which is why the exhortation was necessary. Robertson takes the same two classes from the words: the first sins are plain before all, so plain that they receive instant condemnation, while the others dog a man's steps, not manifest at first but coming out plainly at last, as he observes is true of secret sins. Gill puts the upshot bluntly: some men are such open and notorious sinners that there is no need of inquiry about them, or of witnesses to their character — and should such be proposed for the ministry, Timothy would know at once what to do, namely reject them.

The same division holds on the other side, and here the expositors turn warm. Barnes notes that some men's character is so clear that there can be no doubt from their works that they are good, and we need not wait for the day of judgment to determine it; but others are modest, retiring and unobtrusive, and may live in obscurity — yet even these cannot be concealed for ever, since the divine government has its arrangements for bringing out every man's character. Clarke describes the same people with evident affection: though the very holy and very useful cannot be unknown, there are others not less holy who need bringing forward, who do much good in private, and whose good works are not known till after diligent inquiry — these being they who do not let their left hand know what their right hand does. Ellicott hears an encouragement addressed to Timothy's own anxiety, since in his difficult post he might fear that true nobility of character would escape his notice, and the best and truest never be enrolled on the register of church officers. St. Paul bids him take courage: in many a case self-sacrifice, generosity and stern principle will be manifest enough to guide his choice, and where the higher and sweeter virtues are hidden, he may be sure that in God's good season these too will become known, in time to call them into his Master's service.

Two of the witnesses close by admitting how much remains unsettled. Clarke, after what he calls so long and minute an examination, concedes the difficulty: the whole account concerning the widows — who they were, what their provision, what their occupation, and how they were supported — are to him questions of considerable difficulty, and he has given the best account in his power. On the imposition of hands, or what he calls vulgarly but improperly ordination, he records a conviction that separates him from the rest: what is said of it in this chapter, and indeed in the epistle, is rather to be understood prophetically, and was intended for a much later age of the Church. Ellicott records a suggestion made with considerable ingenuity, that the last verse introduces a new division of the Epistle rather than closing this one. Wesley closes where the argument began, taking the hidden good works as those not so manifest, which yet cannot be long hid from Timothy's knowledge — and drawing the same rule from it: on this account also, be not hasty in laying on of hands.
